cards.q: WHO definition of rational use of medicines
cards.a: Drugs suited to clinical needs, at individual doses, for an adequate period, at lowest cost to patient and community

cards.q: Supply-use chain stages covered by rational use: list all
cards.a: Selection; procurement; storage; prescribing; dispensing; monitoring; feedback

cards.q: Criteria of appropriate prescribing: list all
cards.a: Appropriate indication; drug suited to patient (efficacy, tolerability, safety); dose, route, duration fitted to patient; no contraindication and benefit above harm; correct dispensing with information; monitoring of adherence and effects

cards.q: Factors influencing prescribing: list all
cards.a: Prescriber knowledge; role models; heavy patient load; demand for prompt relief; imprecise diagnosis; drug promotion; unethical inducements; patient demands

cards.q: Effect of improving prescriber knowledge alone on rational use
cards.a: Fails to promote it, shown repeatedly

cards.q: Irrational prescribing patterns: list all
cards.a: Drug when none needed; drug unrelated to diagnosis; wrong drug; ineffective drug; wrong route; wrong dose; wrong duration; unnecessary combination; costly drug when cheaper equal; unsafe use; polypharmacy

cards.q: Drugs per prescription, average and maximum
cards.a: Average 3 to 4; some as many as 10 to 12

cards.q: Consequences of irrational prescribing: list all
cards.a: Delayed or lost relief; more adverse effects; longer hospital stay; morbidity and mortality; microbial resistance; financial loss; lost patient trust; perpetuated public health problem

cards.q: Three categories of drug names: list all
cards.a: Chemical name; non-proprietary (generic) name; proprietary (brand) name

cards.q: Chemical name, suitability for prescribing
cards.a: Cumbersome; unsuitable for prescribing

cards.q: Manufacturer code name before approved name
cards.a: Code name, e.g. RO 15-1788 (later flumazenil)

cards.q: Bodies that set non-proprietary names: list all
cards.a: USAN (USA); BAN (Britain); rINN (WHO)

cards.q: Common term for non-proprietary name, and why it is wrong
cards.a: Generic name; etymologically 'generic' should mean chemical or pharmacological group

cards.q: Synonymous non-proprietary names: list all examples
cards.a: Meperidine = pethidine; lidocaine = lignocaine

cards.q: Amlodipine brand names from different manufacturers: list all
cards.a: AMCARD; AMLOVAS; STAMLO

cards.q: Timolol maleate eye drop brand names by country
cards.a: TIMOPTIC (USA); GLUCOMOL (India)

cards.q: Advantages of prescribing by generic name: list all
cards.a: Uniformity; convenience; economy; better comprehension

cards.q: Why generic products cost less than brands
cards.a: No money spent on brand promotion

cards.q: Effect of prescribing by generic name on dispensing
cards.a: Pharmacist may supply any manufacturer's product

cards.q: When brand prescribing is safer
cards.a: Quality and bioavailability consistency matter and official quality control is weak

cards.q: Difference between BNF and National Formulary of India
cards.a: BNF lists brand names with costs; NFI does not

cards.q: Formulary entries for each drug: list all
cards.a: Indications; doses; dosage forms; contraindications; precautions; adverse effects; storage

cards.q: Biotechnology-derived drugs: examples
cards.a: Human growth hormone; human insulin; alteplase; interferon; monoclonal antibodies; erythropoietin

cards.q: Steps of rational prescribing, in order: list all
cards.a: Provisional diagnosis; define therapeutic problems; define goals; select drug class for each goal; select drug on efficacy, safety, suitability and cost; decide route, dose, duration; give information; monitor adherence; monitor goal achievement; modify therapy; monitor adverse effects

cards.q: Information given to patient when prescribing: list all
cards.a: Expected effect and timing; cure or only control; effect of missed doses; common side effects; how and how long to take; tests needed; precautions

cards.q: Precaution examples given to patients: list all
cards.a: Driving after conventional antihistamines; alcohol with metronidazole; standing still after sublingual glyceryl trinitrate

cards.q: Lab-test examples for patient instructions: list all
cards.a: Prothrombin time with coumarin anticoagulants; leucocyte count with anticancer drugs

cards.q: Principle for side-effect counselling
cards.a: Mention common side effects without alarming the patient; omitting them is negligence

cards.q: Final check of patient instruction
cards.a: Ensure the patient has properly understood them

cards.q: Scope of rational prescribing beyond handing over prescription
cards.a: Monitoring, periodic review and changes until goals achieved

cards.q: Rational prescribing steps (Katzung), in order: list all
cards.a: Specific diagnosis; pathophysiology; therapeutic objective; drug of choice; dosing regimen; monitoring plan and endpoint; patient education

cards.q: Main determinant of dosing regimen
cards.a: Pharmacokinetics of the drug in that patient

cards.q: Patient features shaping drug of choice: list all
cards.a: Age; other diseases; other drugs (duplication, interactions); aspirin intolerance or ulcer history; cost and insurance; need for once-daily dosing

cards.q: Current emphasis in choosing drug of choice
cards.a: Precision medicine, using patient characteristics

cards.q: Elements of outpatient prescription, in order: list all
cards.a: Prescriber name, licence class, address, phone; date; patient name and address; drug name; strength; quantity; directions; refills; childproof waiver; warnings; signature; registration numbers

cards.q: Units for strength on prescriptions
cards.a: Metric units

cards.q: Meaning of 20% potassium chloride solution
cards.a: 20 g of KCl per dL (per 100 mL); write concentration and volume out

cards.q: Factors setting prescribed quantity: list all
cards.a: Duration of therapy; cost; need for clinic contact; abuse potential; toxicity or overdose risk; standard pack sizes; new or repeat prescription

cards.q: Quantity for a new chronic-disease drug
cards.a: Small initial quantity with refills, to limit cost if not tolerated

cards.q: Principle for directions to patient
cards.a: Simpler is better, with fewer doses and drugs per day

cards.q: Safer way to write directions
cards.a: Write them out in full, not abbreviated

cards.q: Main cause of treatment failure
cards.a: Patient non-compliance (nonadherence)

cards.q: Errors of omission in orders: examples
cards.a: 'Resume pre-op meds'; 'continue present IV fluids'; 'continue eye drops' with no eye or drug named

cards.q: Leading-zero rule for decimal doses
cards.a: Always put zero before the decimal point: 0.1, not .1

cards.q: Trailing-zero rule for decimal doses
cards.a: Never add trailing zero: write 1 mg, not 1.0 mg (misread as 10)

cards.q: Units abbreviation to avoid, and why
cards.a: Abbreviation U; '10 U' is misread as 100, so write 'units'

cards.q: Microgram abbreviation to avoid, and why
cards.a: 'g' misread as mg (1000-fold overdose); write 'microgram'

cards.q: Slash used as decimal point
cards.a: Abandon it; misread as numeral 1

cards.q: Meaning of OD in prescriptions
cards.a: Right eye only; used for 'every day' it caused wrong-eye dosing

cards.q: Misreading of QD
cards.a: Read as QID: four doses a day instead of one; write 'daily'

cards.q: Order that must not be filled
cards.a: Dosage units without total dose when several unit sizes exist (e.g. one ampule of furosemide)

cards.q: Acronyms to avoid in orders: list all examples
cards.a: ASA (aspirin); 5-ASA; 6MP; write drug names in full

cards.q: Dose size above which a comma is used (USA)
cards.a: Doses over 999

cards.q: Look-alike drug name pairs cited: list all
cards.a: Apixaban and aripiprazole; methotrexate and metolazone

cards.q: Way to prevent look-alike name errors
cards.a: Write the indication in the prescription body

cards.q: Prescribing error categories: list all
cards.a: Omission of needed information; poor writing causing dose or timing errors; inappropriate drug for the situation

cards.q: Causes of inappropriate drug prescription: list all
cards.a: Unrecognised contraindications from other diseases; unknown other drugs including OTC; physicochemical incompatibility

cards.q: Parenteral incompatibility example
cards.a: Certain insulin preparations should not be mixed

cards.q: Absorption interaction example
cards.a: Antacids and metal-rich products impair tetracycline absorption

cards.q: Types of noncompliance: list all
cards.a: Fails to obtain medication; fails to take as prescribed; stops early; another person takes it

cards.q: Factors encouraging noncompliance: list all
cards.a: Symptomless disease; painful chronic conditions; frequent dosing; living alone; hard-to-open packs; lack of transport; cultural or personal beliefs

cards.q: Strategies to improve compliance: list all
cards.a: Patient-team communication; assessing social and economic conditions; routine linked to meals; dose organisers and alarms; refill reminders; active patient participation

cards.q: When medication reconciliation occurs (US)
cards.a: At each level-of-care change, e.g. discharge, and each office visit

cards.q: Traditional US prescribers: list all
cards.a: Physicians; osteopaths; dentists; podiatrists; veterinarians

cards.q: Pharmacist refill rule (US)
cards.a: Cannot refill without prescriber authorisation

cards.q: Refill rule for Schedule II drugs
cards.a: No refills, new prescription needed, several orders allowed up to 90 days

cards.q: Telephone ordering of Schedule II drugs
cards.a: Not permitted

cards.q: Refill rule for Schedules III to V
cards.a: Maximum five refills; none after 6 months from writing

cards.q: US controlled-substance schedules I to V: potential for abuse
cards.a: I high, no accepted medical use; II high, accepted use; III less than II; IV less than III; V less than IV

cards.q: Requirement on every controlled-drug prescription (US)
cards.a: Valid DEA number

cards.q: Legal status of off-label use (US)
cards.a: Not restricted by federal law; FDA approves only labelled uses

cards.q: US drug classes by prescription status: list all
cards.a: Over-the-counter; prescription only (Rx Only)

cards.q: OTC drug definition (US)
cards.a: Safely self-administered for self-limiting conditions, with label understood by laypeople

cards.q: Share of US drug doses that are OTC
cards.a: Half

cards.q: Generic substitution rule (US)
cards.a: Cheapest generic equivalent unless prescriber writes 'dispense as written'

cards.q: Caveat on generic equivalence
cards.a: Bioavailability can vary between manufacturers and sometimes between lots

cards.q: FDA adverse-reaction reporting programme (US)
cards.a: MedWatch, Form FDA 3500

cards.q: NPI identifier (US)
cards.a: 10-digit number issued by NPPES

cards.q: E-prescribed share of US prescriptions
cards.a: 70 percent

cards.q: DEA rule for e-prescribing controlled drugs
cards.a: Only registered prescribers, with identity proofing

cards.q: WHO definition of essential medicines
cards.a: Medicines satisfying the priority health-care needs of the population

cards.q: WHO criteria for selecting essential medicines: list all
cards.a: Public health relevance; evidence of efficacy and safety; comparative cost-effectiveness

cards.q: Availability conditions for essential medicines: list all
cards.a: Available at all times in functioning health systems; adequate amounts; suitable dosage forms; assured quality; adequate information; affordable price

cards.q: Choosing between two similar medicines
cards.a: Compare efficacy, safety, quality, price and availability; cost-benefit is a major factor

cards.q: When fixed-ratio combinations qualify as essential
cards.a: Each ingredient dose fits the population and the combination has a proven advantage

cards.q: Form of most essential medicines
cards.a: Single compounds

cards.q: Year of first WHO model list of essential drugs
Size of WHO 20th model list (2017)
cards.a: 433 medicines, including 25 FDCs

cards.q: Year of India's first National Essential Drugs List
Size of India's National List of Essential Medicines (2015)
cards.a: 376 medicines, 20 of them FDCs

cards.q: Levels of health care in India's NLEM 2015: list all
cards.a: Primary; secondary; tertiary

cards.q: Benefits of adopting essential-medicine lists: list all
cards.a: Improved availability; cost saving; more rational use

cards.q: Orphan drug definition
cards.a: Drug for a rare disease, or disease endemic only in poor countries, where sales will not recoup development cost

cards.q: US rare-disease threshold (Orphan Drug Amendment Act 1983)
cards.a: Fewer than 0.2 million people in the USA

cards.q: Government support for orphan drugs
cards.a: Tax benefits and other incentives

cards.q: OTC drug examples: list all
cards.a: Paracetamol; aspirin; antacids; senna; lactulose; vitamins; ferrous salts

cards.q: Indian rule placing prescription drugs
cards.a: Schedule H, Drugs and Cosmetics Rules (1945), as amended

cards.q: Sale status of antibiotics (India)
cards.a: Prescription only; all antibiotics included

cards.q: Rational fixed-dose combinations: list all examples
cards.a: Sulfamethoxazole + trimethoprim; levodopa + carbidopa or benserazide; combined oral contraceptives; isoniazid + rifampin; amlodipine + atenolol; thiazide + potassium-sparing diuretic

cards.q: Advantages of rational FDCs: list all
cards.a: Convenience and compliance; synergy; additive effect with different side effects; one drug offsets another's side effect; single drug avoided in TB, HIV, falciparum malaria; sometimes cheaper

cards.q: Disadvantages of FDCs: list all
cards.a: Unneeded drug adds side effects and cost; dose cannot be individualised; different time courses; renal or hepatic change affects components differently; adverse effect hard to attribute; one contraindication bars whole product; false sense of superiority, especially with antimicrobials

cards.q: Decision rule for prescribing any combination
cards.a: If one ingredient is unnecessary, do not prescribe the combination

cards.q: Drug class never combined with others for internal use
cards.a: Corticosteroids (except metered-dose and dry-powder inhalers)

cards.q: Combinations available at more than one dose ratio: examples
cards.a: Levodopa 100 mg + carbidopa 10 or 25 mg; amoxicillin 250 or 500 mg + clavulanic acid 125 mg

cards.q: Recently banned irrational FDCs in India
cards.a: 344, in addition to earlier bans

cards.q: Why too many FDCs exist
cards.a: Industry produces and vigorously promotes them; only a handful are rational

cards.q: Synergy basis of sulfamethoxazole plus trimethoprim
cards.a: Inhibit sequential steps in microbial folate synthesis

cards.q: Drugs with low safety margin where TDM helps: list all
cards.a: Digoxin; anticonvulsants; antiarrhythmics; theophylline; aminoglycosides; lithium; tricyclic antidepressants

cards.q: Other TDM indications: list all
cards.a: Large individual variation; toxic drugs in renal failure; poisoning; unexplained treatment failure; checking compliance

cards.q: Drug groups where plasma-level monitoring is of no value: list all
cards.a: Easily measured response (antihypertensives, oral anticoagulants); prodrugs activated in body (levodopa); hit-and-run drugs (reserpine, MAO inhibitors, omeprazole); irreversible action (organophosphates, phenoxybenzamine)

cards.q: Hit-and-run drug defining feature
cards.a: Effect lasts longer than the drug itself

cards.q: Sampling time for dose adjustment of long-acting drugs
cards.a: Trough steady-state level, just before next dose

cards.q: What the trough level depends on
cards.a: Volume of distribution and clearance

cards.q: Sampling time for short-acting drugs (e.g. ampicillin, gentamicin)
cards.a: Peak, 1 to 2 h after oral or i.m. dose

cards.q: Sampling in suspected poisoning
cards.a: Earliest sample to confirm; repeat to gauge clearance and need for haemodialysis

cards.q: Compliance check by plasma levels
cards.a: Even random sampling is informative

cards.q: Benefits of prolonged-action formulations: list all
cards.a: Less frequent dosing; better adherence; fewer peak-related side effects; smoother control; overnight effect without disturbing sleep

cards.q: Half-life threshold for controlled-release formulations
cards.a: Under 4 h suits them; over 12 h needs none

cards.q: Duration added by membrane-controlled release tablets
cards.a: Only 4 to 8 hours, as drug reaches the colon

cards.q: Drugs needing no prolonged formulation: examples
cards.a: Brief-effect hypnotics and headache remedies; inherently long-acting doxycycline, omeprazole, digoxin, amlodipine

cards.q: Pharmacoeconomics definition
cards.a: Branch of health economics quantifying cost and benefit of therapeutic drugs

cards.q: Main controversy in pharmacoeconomics
cards.a: It puts a monetary value on health and longevity

cards.q: Regulators' added requirement for licensing
cards.a: Economic analysis as well as evidence of individual benefit

cards.q: QALY definition
cards.a: Quality-adjusted life year: survival combined with quality of life, one overall benefit measure

cards.q: Clinical outcome measures: list all
cards.a: Physiological measures; subjective assessments; long-term outcome; quality-of-life measures; QALYs

cards.q: Surrogate end-point hazard (CAST trial)
cards.a: Antiarrhythmics suppressed arrhythmias but increased mortality compared with placebo

cards.q: Number needed to treat (NNT)
cards.a: Number of patients who must be treated for one to show the effect, benefit or harm

cards.q: Placebo response frequency
cards.a: Beneficial effect in about one-third of patients

cards.q: Meta-analysis purpose
cards.a: Statistically pools data from several independent trials

cards.q: Approval needed for experiments on human subjects
cards.a: Independent ethics committee

cards.q: Term for sensible clinical use of existing antibacterials
cards.a: Antibiotic stewardship

cards.q: Basis of antibiotic stewardship
cards.a: Understanding how resistance genes arise and spread

cards.q: Antibiotic stewardship principles: list all
cards.a: Narrower spectrum when other factors equal; de-escalate once pathogen known; monotherapy for definitive treatment; weigh prophylaxis against resistance, microbiome damage, toxicity and cost

cards.q: Definitive-therapy spectrum preference
cards.a: Narrow spectrum: more effective and less disturbance of normal flora

cards.q: Role of broad-spectrum drugs
cards.a: Empirical therapy, to cover all likely pathogens

cards.q: Empirical therapy steps, in order: list all
cards.a: Make at least a tentative diagnosis; guess the likely pathogen; start a specific drug; broad cover only if severe or no diagnostics; narrow or change on bacteriology, avoiding hasty switches

cards.q: Broad empirical regimens when no bacteriology: examples
cards.a: Fluoroquinolone; tetracycline; gentamicin plus a cephalosporin, with metronidazole or clindamycin if anaerobes suspected

cards.q: Serious infection when culture is available but treatment cannot wait
cards.a: Collect specimens, start empirical therapy, change later on bacteriology if response inadequate

cards.q: Chronic infection with time to culture (e.g. chronic UTI)
cards.a: Wait for culture and sensitivity, then start definitive therapy

cards.q: Situations where bactericidal drugs are clearly superior: list all
cards.a: Impaired host defence; life-threatening infection; SABE or less accessible sites; carrier state (e.g. typhoid)

cards.q: Post-antibiotic effect (PAE)
cards.a: Growth suppression that persists after brief exposure, typical of bactericidal drugs

cards.q: Concentration-dependent antimicrobials: examples
cards.a: Aminoglycosides; fluoroquinolones; metronidazole

cards.q: Time-dependent antimicrobials: examples
cards.a: Beta-lactams; glycopeptides; macrolides

cards.q: Dosing advice for concentration-dependent drugs
cards.a: Single daily dose beats divided doses (e.g. gentamicin)

cards.q: Choice by relative toxicity: examples
cards.a: Beta-lactam over aminoglycoside; erythromycin over clindamycin

cards.q: Antibiotics reaching high CSF concentration: examples
cards.a: Cefuroxime; ceftriaxone; chloramphenicol; ciprofloxacin

cards.q: Antibiotics that penetrate CSF poorly
cards.a: Penicillins and aminoglycosides, unless meninges inflamed

cards.q: Mixed infections needing two or more agents: examples
cards.a: Bronchiectasis; peritonitis; some UTIs; brain abscess; diabetic foot; bedsores; gynaecological infections

cards.q: Anaerobe cover added to empirical regimen
cards.a: Clindamycin or metronidazole

cards.q: Combinations to prevent resistance in chronic infection: examples
cards.a: Tuberculosis; leprosy; HIV; H. pylori; malaria

cards.q: Resistance chance for two unrelated drugs (KDT example)
cards.a: About 1 in 10^12 bacilli, from independent mutation rates of 10^-5 and 10^-7

cards.q: Topical antimicrobial combinations: examples
cards.a: Bacitracin; neomycin; polymyxin B

cards.q: Disadvantages of antimicrobial combinations: list all
cards.a: Casual diagnosis; more adverse effects (vancomycin with aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity); superinfection; resistance from underdosed non-synergistic drugs; higher cost

cards.q: Whether severity alone justifies combination when organism is known
cards.a: No; severity alone is not an indication

cards.q: When empirical combination should stop
cards.a: When bacteriological data are available

cards.q: Empirical combinations for severe infection: examples
cards.a: Penicillin + gentamicin; cephalosporin or erythromycin + aminoglycoside; metronidazole or clindamycin if anaerobes

cards.q: Prophylaxis against rheumatic fever recurrence
cards.a: Benzathine penicillin, against group A streptococci

cards.q: TB contact prophylaxis
cards.a: Isoniazid alone for 6 months

cards.q: Difference between prophylaxis and treatment
cards.a: Prophylaxis covers all likely organisms; treatment targets the infecting organism

cards.q: Early targeted treatment of infection found on a test before symptoms, in a high-risk patient
cards.a: Pre-emptive therapy (not prophylaxis)

cards.q: Purpose of suppressive therapy
cards.a: Continue a lower-dose or different antibiotic after infection is controlled but not eradicated

cards.q: Reason patients may get empiric therapy for the whole course
cards.a: Organism never identified, so empiric therapy continues throughout

cards.q: Early pathogen clue for tailoring therapy
cards.a: Gram stain of infected secretion or fluid

cards.q: Reasons for combination in definitive therapy: list all
cards.a: Prevent resistance to monotherapy (e.g. HIV, active TB); reduce toxicity by lowering the dose of one drug

cards.q: Monotherapy vs combinations, definitive therapy
cards.a: Monotherapy preferred unless compelling data favour combination

cards.q: Meaning of the P in P-drug
cards.a: Personal (drugs chosen for regular prescribing)

cards.q: Drugs a physician needs routinely in practice
cards.a: About 40 to 60 drugs

cards.q: Treatment of first choice for a given illness
cards.a: P-treatment

cards.q: Example of P-treatment that uses no drug
cards.a: Lifestyle modification in obesity

cards.q: Criteria for choosing a P-drug
cards.a: Efficacy, safety, suitability for the patient and cost

cards.q: Physician-kept list of P-drugs
cards.a: Pocket P-drug formulary

cards.q: Contents of a pocket P-drug formulary
cards.a: Dosage form, dose, frequency, duration, patient teaching and monitoring

cards.q: How often a P-drug list should be revised
cards.a: From time to time, as new drugs appear

cards.q: Concept essential for rational prescribing and continued medical education
cards.a: P-drug concept

cards.q: Problem when an adverse effect occurs on an FDC
cards.a: Cannot be ascribed to the particular drug causing it

cards.q: Effect of allergy or contraindication to one FDC component
cards.a: Contraindicates the whole product

cards.q: Effect of renal or hepatic impairment on FDC components
cards.a: Pharmacokinetics of components affected differently

cards.q: Time-course problem of FDCs
cards.a: Components given at same interval though their duration of action differs

cards.q: False impression fostered by FDCs, especially antimicrobials
cards.a: Superiority of two drugs over one

cards.q: Antibiotic for non-specific diarrhoea or viral fever
cards.a: Irrational: drug used when none is needed

cards.q: Proton pump inhibitor for any abdominal symptom
cards.a: Irrational: drug unrelated to the diagnosis

cards.q: Routine addition of vitamins or tonics
cards.a: Irrational compulsive coprescription

cards.q: Antibiotic given before infection to cover all likely organisms
cards.a: Primary prophylaxis (not pre-emptive therapy)

cards.q: Why plasma level is useless for a prodrug like levodopa
cards.a: Effect depends on activation, not on plasma level of the given drug

cards.q: Legal requirement on every medicine label
cards.a: Date of manufacture and expiry date

cards.q: What an expiry date means
cards.a: Quality is not assured beyond it; it does not prove the drug has become toxic or lost potency

cards.q: Typical life period of medicines under Schedule P (Rule 96)
cards.a: Mostly 1 to 5 years

cards.q: Longest expiry a manufacturer may set (unless licensing authority accepts stability proof)
cards.a: 5 years

cards.q: Outdated tetracycline capsules: toxicity produced
cards.a: Renal tubular damage resembling Fanconi syndrome (early 1960s); since reformulated

cards.q: Factors that speed loss of potency: list all
cards.a: High humidity; high temperature; liquid forms (less stable than solid dosage forms)

cards.q: Evidence-based medicine: definition
cards.a: Systematic finding, evaluation and use of current research as the basis of clinical decisions

cards.q: Components of therapeutic evaluation of a drug: list all
cards.a: Quantitated benefit; best way to use it (dose, duration, patient selection); comparison with other drugs; surveillance of adverse effects

cards.q: Types of clinical study named: list all
cards.a: Clinical trials; cohort studies; case-control studies

cards.q: Control group in a clinical trial: what it receives
cards.a: Placebo (if ethically permissible) or the existing standard treatment (active control)

cards.q: Cross-over trial design: how subjects serve as controls
cards.a: Each patient receives drug A then B (or reverse), so individual variation is avoided and sample size may fall

cards.q: Use of a drug outside its approved indication, route or dose
cards.a: Off-label use

cards.q: Off-label indication of clonidine
cards.a: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder

cards.q: Diazepam injection used rectally off-label
cards.a: Febrile convulsions and status epilepticus

cards.q: Off-label topical use of azathioprine
cards.a: Psoriasis and atopic dermatitis

cards.q: Off-label use of erythromycin
cards.a: Gastroparesis

cards.q: Off-label use of SSRIs
cards.a: Fibromyalgia and pathological gambling

cards.q: Appetite stimulant used off-label in anorectic patients
cards.a: Cyproheptadine (avoid in underweight children: CNS depression)

cards.q: Off-label use of phentolamine
cards.a: Autonomic hyperreflexia after spinal cord transection

cards.q: US rule on prescribing for any reasonable purpose
cards.a: Allowed; insurers may refuse payment without compendium support

cards.q: Off-label prescribing risk for the physician
cards.a: Litigation if untoward effects follow

cards.q: Promotion aimed directly at doctors
cards.a: Direct-to-physician marketing (DTP)

cards.q: Disadvantage of promotional product literature
cards.a: Biased or misleading content; artificial demand; brand monopoly

cards.q: Prescriber factor: copying teachers or popular doctors
cards.a: Role models

cards.q: Prescriber factor: heavy workload
cards.a: Routinised symptom-based prescribing

cards.q: Prescriber factor: medicine given to cover all causes
cards.a: Imprecise diagnosis

cards.q: Industry inducements to doctors
cards.a: Gifts, dinner parties, conference delegation

cards.q: Patient belief behind demand for medicine
cards.a: Belief that every complaint needs a drug

cards.q: Does improving prescriber knowledge alone ensure rational use?
cards.a: No; repeatedly shown to fail

cards.q: Indian schedule for prescription-only drugs
cards.a: Schedule H, Drugs and Cosmetics Rules 1945

cards.q: OTC examples in India (relatively harmless)
cards.a: Paracetamol, aspirin, antacids, senna, lactulose, vitamins, ferrous salts

cards.q: Schedule X storage requirement
cards.a: Lock and key

cards.q: Schedule X prescription retention
cards.a: Duplicate; copy kept at least 2 years

cards.q: Substitution allowed for Schedule X?
cards.a: No substitute or alternative drug

cards.q: Schedule X examples
cards.a: Amphetamine, psychotropic drugs, barbiturates, methaqualone, glutethimide

cards.q: Reclassifying a prescription drug as OTC
cards.a: Switch (prescription-to-OTC)

cards.q: Switch criterion for a drug
cards.a: Consumer can self-diagnose and safely self-treat

cards.q: Statins refused OTC status
cards.a: Lovastatin and pravastatin: chronic hyperlipidaemia needs professional care

cards.q: Oral acyclovir refused OTC for genital herpes
cards.a: Misdiagnosis and viral resistance concerns

cards.q: Naloxone nasal spray OTC switch year
cards.a: 2023 (US), for opioid overdose

cards.q: Norgestrel OTC switch purpose
cards.a: Prevention of pregnancy (2023)

cards.q: Prescription drugs considered for future OTC switch
cards.a: Sumatriptan, nicotine replacement therapy, varenicline

cards.q: Which older anorectic drug has been discontinued in the US?
cards.a: Phenylpropanolamine (with mazindol and phenmetrazine)

cards.q: OTC antitussive abused at high doses
cards.a: Dextromethorphan

cards.q: WHO term for deliberately, fraudulently mislabelled medicine
cards.a: Counterfeit medicine

cards.q: Spurious drug: manufactured under another drug's name
cards.a: Drugs and Cosmetics Act s.17B

cards.q: Counterfeit with correct ingredient but wrong amount, example
cards.a: Glibenclamide tablets with several times the normal dose (Tanzania)

cards.q: Smuggled genuine-looking drugs, example
cards.a: Viagra and Cialis smuggled into Thailand

cards.q: Genuine packaging with undeclared ingredients, example
cards.a: Orlistat tablets sold in USA

cards.q: Track-and-trace coding on each pack
cards.a: Mass serialisation

cards.q: Anti-counterfeit technologies
cards.a: Forensic markers, cloud supply-chain data, blockchain

cards.q: 2018 DTAB advice for top brands
